diagnostic_evidence.quote: The set-valued map \(\solp\) has nonempty values and is locally bounded.

To this end, we show that the expression \eqref{form:asm} carries strong variational information whenever the Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification holds and all the mappings $F,G,H$ belong to a common o-minimal structure (for example, are semialgebraic).

issues.failure_explanation: Definability and MFCQ do not suffice, even when minimizers exist and are bounded separately at every parameter. For the unconstrained polynomial objective F(x,theta)=x^2(theta x-1)^2-theta x, every parameter has a nonempty bounded minimizer set. Nevertheless, f(0)=0 and f(theta)≤-1 for every nonzero theta, by evaluating at x=1/theta. Thus f is discontinuous and cannot have a conservative field as defined in the paper. The omitted local boundedness assumption excludes this behavior.

failure_location.quote: Definable parametric optimization problems with possibly nonsmooth objectives, inequality constraints, and non-unique primal and dual solutions admit an adjoint state formula under a mere qualification condition.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Include existence and local boundedness of the primal solution multifunction in the advertised sufficient conditions, consistently with the standing assumptions.
issues.overall_effect: The abstract and introduction advertise a broader sufficiency result than the formal theorems establish.
issues.title: The advertised sufficiency of qualification alone omits essential optimizer stability
issues.why_classification: This requires an essential restriction of the advertised scope, but the paper's formally stated main results and their proof architecture can remain unchanged.

issues.failure_explanation: The stated condition concerns only x*, while F is assumed merely locally Lipschitz. For F(x,theta)=x^2+|theta|, the unique optimizer x*(theta)=0 is differentiable everywhere, but f(theta)=|theta| is not differentiable at zero and the displayed classical gradients of F are unavailable there.

failure_location.quote: if the mapping $\theta \mapsto x^*(\theta)$ were differentiable, the chain rule would give

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Require F to be differentiable at the relevant optimizer-parameter pair, or explicitly restrict this introductory calculation to the continuously differentiable setting.
issues.overall_effect: The introductory classical chain-rule implication is false under its stated conditions; the later smooth-case assumptions already avoid this problem.
issues.title: Differentiability of the optimizer selection does not justify the introductory chain rule
issues.why_classification: A standard local smoothness condition repairs this preliminary calculation without altering any of the substantive nonsmooth results.

issues.failure_explanation: The displayed joint formula uses every column of the constraint Jacobian but never requires inactive multipliers to vanish. Take g1(x,theta)=x and g2(x,theta)=-x-1 at x=0, with no equalities. MFCQ holds with d=-1, but lambda=(1,1) makes the full joint Jacobian combination zero while the active multiplier lambda1 is nonzero.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add lambda_i=0 for inactive constraints, or restrict the Jacobian combination to active constraints.
issues.overall_effect: The displayed implication is false. The intended joint MFCQ conclusion used later remains valid for complementary multipliers.
issues.title: The joint MFCQ implication permits nonzero inactive multipliers
issues.why_classification: Adding the missing complementarity restriction is a short local repair and preserves the intended qualification result and its applications.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The following assumptions hold throughout the current section, Section~\myref{sect:diffcase}.
The constraints are expressed equivalently $\pvar_1 \leq 0$ and $\pvar_2 \leq - |\param|$.

issues.failure_explanation: For every theta, all points (0,x2) with x2≤-|theta| are minimizers, so the solution set is unbounded. Moreover, at theta=0 the union of all adjoint outputs is the whole real line: take x=(-a,0), lambda2+lambda3=a, and vary a≥0. Consequently, this all-output map is not locally bounded and is not a conservative field under the paper's definition.

failure_location.quote: The following example shows that the (Clarke) subdifferential cannot capture all the information of the output of the adjoint formula in \myref{alg:asm} as the latter may produce artifacts which do not carry any standard variational meaning.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the harmless lower bounds x1≥-2 and x2≥-1-theta^2. They preserve feasibility for every parameter, MFCQ, the zero value function, and the displayed artifact while making the solution multifunction locally bounded.
issues.overall_effect: The example is outside the stated standing setting and cannot illustrate a conservative all-output field there. Its individual non-Clarke adjoint calculation remains correct.
issues.title: The smooth artifact example violates the section's bounded-solution assumption
issues.why_classification: Two routine bounding constraints place the example inside the advertised class without losing any of its substantive illustrative properties.

issues.failure_explanation: The gradient of L1 includes its multiplier derivatives, which equal G and H. An inactive inequality has G_i<0, so a KKT solution is not a zero of this full gradient. For example, minimizing x^2 subject to x-1≤0 gives the unique smooth primal-dual solution (x,lambda)=(0,0), but the full L1 gradient is (0,-1). Thus the stated implicit-function procedure cannot be applied even in this regular example.

failure_location.quote: The second is \emph{implicit differentiation}, where the implicit function theorem is applied to the critical condition \(\nabla \Lcal_{1}(\solvpd(\bar{\param})) = 0\)

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Differentiate a correct complementary KKT system, or first restrict to a locally fixed active set and set inactive multipliers to zero. State the required regularity conditions and base the cost comparison on that system.
issues.overall_effect: The described implicit-differentiation comparator and its associated cost discussion do not cover ordinary solutions with inactive inequalities.
issues.title: Implicit differentiation is applied to a system that is not the inequality KKT system
issues.why_classification: The implicit system must be reformulated, rather than merely relabelled, but this is a contained correction that does not alter the adjoint method itself.

issues.failure_explanation: Differentiating a selected solution branch does not require the optimization problem to have a unique solution. For F(x,theta)=(x^2-1)^2+theta^2, both ±1 are global minimizers, but the solver selection x*(theta)=1 is smooth and can be differentiated automatically. Implicit differentiation also applies locally at either branch because F_xx=8 there. Local nonsingularity or branch uniqueness is not global uniqueness of the optimizer set.

failure_location.quote: In terms of assumptions, it is immediately apparent that both methods require the uniqueness and differentiability of the solutions, while \myref{alg:asm} does not.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State conditions on the selected solver branch and, for implicit differentiation, on an appropriate locally nonsingular KKT system, without requiring global optimizer uniqueness.
issues.overall_effect: The paper overstates the uniqueness advantage of ASM over both comparison methods.
issues.title: The comparison incorrectly makes global solution uniqueness necessary
issues.why_classification: A substantive comparative necessity claim must be withdrawn, although a comparable discussion of the methods' differing regularity requirements survives.

issues.failure_explanation: Comparing upper bounds does not prove an ordering of actual worst-case costs. Even the displayed ASM and AD bounds are not universally ordered: no general inequality relates Cost(solver_pd) to Cost(solver_p), or Cost(L) to the remaining AD costs. The text supplies only typical-case statements about those quantities.

failure_location.quote: Comparing with Equations~\eqref{eq:costasm}, it is obvious that the worst case computational cost of \myref{alg:asm} is lower, and possibly much lower, than either automatic differentiation or implicit differentiation, making it a strong competitor for the purpose of differentiating the value function of nonlinear programs.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Retain the cost formulas as conditional estimates and describe ASM as potentially cheaper when multiplier retrieval is inexpensive and Lagrangian differentiation is cheap relative to solving the problem.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed unconditional computational dominance is unsupported by the operation-count estimates.
issues.title: Upper cost bounds do not establish the asserted worst-case ordering
issues.why_classification: The uniform ranking must be weakened, but the supported cost estimates and conditional practical advantage remain available without new proof architecture.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The MFCQ is satisfied at any \((\param, \pvar) \in \graph R\), i.e., the MFCQ holds throughout the feasible set \(R(\param)\) for any \(\param \in \Rd\).

issues.failure_explanation: The standing assumption requires partial-in-x MFCQ simultaneously for every parameter. Consider the polynomial constraint g_delta(x,theta)=x^3-theta-delta≤0, where delta is the scalar diagonal perturbation, and objective F=x^2. For every delta, the feasible optimizer x=0 at theta=-delta has an active constraint with g_delta,x=0, so MFCQ fails. Minimizers nevertheless exist and are locally bounded for every delta. Thus every perturbation is bad for the uniform assumption, even though joint-in-(x,theta) qualification holds.

failure_location.quote: The authors in \cite{bolte2018qualification} proved that, for diagonally perturbed definable programming, the Assumption~\myhyperref{ass:standing}{ass:a2} is generic, i.e., the MFCQ holds throughout the feasible set for all but finitely many (hence for Lebesgue-almost all) diagonal perturbations

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Withdraw the uniform genericity assertion. Any retained fixed-parameter genericity statement must allow its exceptional perturbations to depend on theta and must not be presented as establishing the standing assumption.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed genericity of the uniform standing qualification assumption is false; the main theorems may still assume it directly.
issues.title: Diagonal perturbations need not generically enforce MFCQ uniformly in the parameter
issues.why_classification: The central uniform quantifier cannot be preserved: the counterexample has no successful diagonal perturbation at all. Repair necessarily abandons the advertised uniform genericity guarantee.

issues.failure_explanation: The theorem and multiplier definition use conv D_F, but the proof defines D_L using raw D_F and ultimately identifies their zero slices. These slices can differ, including in nonemptiness. For unconstrained F(x,theta)=|x|, take D_F(0,theta)={(-1,0),(1,0)} and the ordinary gradient elsewhere. This is a definable conservative field. At the optimizer x=0, the theorem's D_f is {0}, whereas the raw D_L has no element with zero x component. The final identification and the use of the convexified density lemma are therefore invalid.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Convexify D_F at the start of the proof and define D_L accordingly. Convexification preserves the required field properties, and the chain rule extends by linearity.
issues.overall_effect: The proof does not establish the theorem for genuinely nonconvex conservative fields. The smooth and Clarke-field subcases do not suffer this particular gap.
issues.title: The main proof drops the convexification needed for stationarity
issues.why_classification: A standard local convexification step repairs the proof while preserving the complete theorem and all its guarantees.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \(\consv_{\varphi}\colon \Rell \to \Rell\) be a locally bounded and graph closed set-valued map with nonempty values.

issues.failure_explanation: Pointwise inclusion does not preserve joint closed-graph behavior. Let theta=(t,s), F(x,t,s)=|x|-|x-t|, and impose H=x-t/2-s=0. All standing assumptions hold. Using partial Clarke multipliers, at t>0,s=0 the unique multiplier is mu=-2 and the adjoint output is (0,2). At (t,s)=(0,0), the partial function F(·,0,0) is identically zero, forcing mu=0; all resulting adjoint outputs have the form (a,0), with -1≤a≤1. Hence the proposed modified field is not graph closed.

failure_location.quote: Optionally, for any \(\param \in \Rq\), we can replace \(\consv_{F(\cdot,\param)}\) by the Clarke partial subdifferential  \(\clarkep{\pvar}F(\cdot, \param)\), which is contained in the projection of the joint sudifferential \cite[Proposition 2.3.16]{clarke1983nonsmooth}.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: After forming the reduced adjoint map, take the closure of its graph. This closure remains contained in the original closed conservative field, is locally bounded and definable, and contains every proposed output.
issues.overall_effect: The optional substitution does not preserve the conclusion that the displayed adjoint map is itself a conservative field. The original construction using the joint projection is unaffected.
issues.title: Replacing joint projections by partial Clarke subdifferentials can destroy closedness
issues.why_classification: A modified field construction is required, but it is contained and preserves the oracle outputs and the main theorem's scope.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let \(A \subset \R^{M}\) be closed with empty interior.

issues.failure_explanation: The hypotheses allow A to be empty, but no sequence indexed by the natural numbers can take its values in the empty set. Thus the proof's initial object is undefined for an allowed input, although the lemma's conclusion can still be obtained in that case.

failure_location.quote: Since every subset of \(\R^{M}\) is itself separable, there exists a sequence \((c_r)_{r\in\N} \subset A\) which is dense in \(A\).

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Handle A=empty first by choosing a distinct sequence escaping to infinity, and then assume A is nonempty for the displayed construction.
issues.overall_effect: The proof does not cover the empty-set case. The nonempty fractal application is unaffected.
issues.title: The accumulation-sequence proof assumes the closed set is nonempty
issues.why_classification: A one-line degenerate-case construction preserves the lemma and every application.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: For any \(k \in \N\), consider \(\Bcal(z_k,r_k)\) such that \(r_k > 0\), \(r_k \xrightarrow[k \to \infny]{} 0\), and \(\Bcal(z_k,r_k) \cap \Bcal(z_{s},r_{s}) = \varnothing\) for \(s \neq k\).

issues.failure_explanation: Disjointness and r_k→0 do not make bump heights negligible relative to distance from C. For C={0} in R^2, choose z_k=(2^{-k},0), r_k=2^{-k}/8, and bar f(z)=||z||^2. These balls satisfy the stated conditions, but bar g(z_k)/||z_k|| tends to phi(0)/8>0. Since bar g is nonnegative and vanishes at zero, differentiability there would require derivative zero, contradicting this quotient.

failure_location.quote: Moreover  \(\bar{g}\) is differentiable and locally Lipschitz on \(\Rell\).

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Shrink the radii further so that r_k≤dist(z_k,C)/(k+2), while retaining disjointness and convergence to zero. Then verify that the bump contribution is o(||z-c||) at every c in C; the unit-gradient calculation at the rescaled bump points is unchanged.
issues.overall_effect: The pointwise differentiability assertions in the supporting construction and the nondefinable counterexample are not established by the chosen radii.
issues.title: Disjoint shrinking bumps need not be differentiable on their accumulation set
issues.why_classification: The radii are already free construction parameters. A routine additional shrinking condition and a local estimate restore differentiability without changing any claimed property or downstream guarantee.
